svg.title: Inline Mermaid appears after the reply
svg.desc: Two captured paragraphs explaining a CI pipeline appear first. The same reply then gains its complete terminal Mermaid chart. Each frame lasts 2.5 seconds.

The runner checks out the code, installs
 dependencies, and runs linting and the test suite, usually with unit tests first and slower integration tests after. If any stage fails, the run
 stops, the commit is marked red, the author is notified, and nothing downstream happens; the fix is a new commit that starts a fresh run. If
 everything passes, the pipeline builds an immutable artifact such as a container image tagged with the commit hash, pushes it to a registry, and
 deploys it to a staging environment where smoke tests or end-to-end checks run against the real stack.

 A production deploy then happens either automatically on merge to the main branch or after a manual approval gate. The new artifact rolls out
 gradually, often to a canary slice or in a blue-green swap, while health checks and error-rate metrics are watched. If those degrade, or an operator
 spots a problem, the rollback is simply redeploying the previous artifact, which is still in the registry and already proven healthy; because
 builds are immutable, no rebuild is needed and the revert takes seconds. The bad commit stays in history, a fix lands as a new commit, and the whole
 pipeline runs again from the top.

g.text: A push lands on the remote, which fires a webhook that starts a pipeline run against that exact commit. The runner checks out the code, installs
dependencies, and runs linting and the test suite, usually with unit tests first and slower integration tests after. If any stage fails, the run
stops, the commit is marked red, the author is notified, and nothing downstream happens; the fix is a new commit that starts a fresh run. If
everything passes, the pipeline builds an immutable artifact such as a container image tagged with the commit hash, pushes it to a registry, and
deploys it to a staging environment where smoke tests or end-to-end checks run against the real stack.
A production deploy then happens either automatically on merge to the main branch or after a manual approval gate. The new artifact rolls out
gradually, often to a canary slice or in a blue-green swap, while health checks and error-rate metrics are watched. If those degrade, or an operator
spots a problem, the rollback is simply redeploying the previous artifact, which is still in the registry and already proven healthy; because
builds are immutable, no rebuild is needed and the revert takes seconds. The bad commit stays in history, a fix lands as a new commit, and the whole
pipeline runs again from the top.

dependencies, and runs linting and the test suite, usually with unit tests first and slower integration tests after. If any stage fails, the run
stops, the commit is marked red, the author is notified, and nothing downstream happens; the fix is a new commit that starts a fresh run. If
everything passes, the pipeline builds an immutable artifact such as a container image tagged with the commit hash, pushes it to a registry, and
deploys it to a staging environment where smoke tests or end-to-end checks run against the real stack.
A production deploy then happens either automatically on merge to the main branch or after a manual approval gate. The new artifact rolls out
gradually, often to a canary slice or in a blue-green swap, while health checks and error-rate metrics are watched. If those degrade, or an operator
spots a problem, the rollback is simply redeploying the previous artifact, which is still in the registry and already proven healthy; because
builds are immutable, no rebuild is needed and the revert takes seconds. The bad commit stays in history, a fix lands as a new commit, and the whole
pipeline runs again from the top.
